nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a normed ring, $\sigma$ an index type and $c : \sigma \to \R$. A power series $f = \sum_t a_t x^t \in R[[x_i : i \in \sigma]]$ is \emph{restricted for $c$} if \[ \lVert a_t \rVert \prod_{i} c_i^{\,t_i} \longrightarrow 0 \] along the cofinite filter on the multidegrees $t$.
nodes.label: def:isrestricted

nodes.statement: $f$ is restricted for $c$ if and only if it is restricted for $\lvert c \rvert$.
nodes.label: lem:isrestricted-abs

nodes.statement: A power series with finitely many nonzero coefficients is restricted for every $c$; in particular every polynomial is.
nodes.label: lem:isrestricted-finite-support

nodes.statement: The restricted series for a fixed $c$ form a subring of $R[[x_i]]$. We write $R_c\langle x_i : i \in \sigma\rangle$, or $\mathrm{Restricted}\ R\ c$, for it.
nodes.label: prop:restricted-ring

nodes.statement: Closure under subtraction is the usual squeeze. Multiplication is the interesting axiom: the coefficients of a product are antidiagonal sums, \[ (fg)_t = \sum_{u + w = t} a_u b_w , \] and it is not immediate that these tend to $0$. They do, because for each $t$ the antidiagonal is finite and the norm of the sum is bounded by the maximum of $\lVert a_u \rVert c^u \cdot \lVert b_w \rVert c^w$ over it; given $\varepsilon$, all but finitely many $u$ have $\lVert a_u\rVert c^u$ small and all but finitely many $w$ have $\lVert b_w \rVert c^w$ small, and a multidegree $t$ outside a suitable finite set cannot be split with both parts in the exceptional sets.

Monomials, constants and variables are restricted, giving $\mathrm{monomial}$, $C$ and $X$ in $R_c\langle x\rangle$, and the inclusion $\mathrm{toRestricted}$ of the polynomial ring, which is an injective ring homomorphism.
nodes.label: def:restricted-elements

nodes.statement: A norm-nonincreasing ring homomorphism $R \to S$ induces $R_c\langle x\rangle \to S_c\langle x\rangle$ coefficientwise.
nodes.label: def:restricted-map

nodes.statement: The one-variable case is the specialisation of Definition~\ref{def:isrestricted} to a one-element index type. When moreover $R = K$ is a complete nonarchimedean field and $c = 1$, the ring $K\langle x \rangle$ is the \emph{Tate algebra} $T_1$.
nodes.label: def:tate-algebra

nodes.statement: The \emph{Gauss norm} of $f$ at radius $c$ is \[ \lVert f \rVert_c = \sup_t \; \lVert a_t \rVert \prod_i c_i^{\,t_i}, \] when the supremum is finite; the predicate $\mathrm{HasGaussNorm}$ records finiteness.
nodes.label: def:gaussnorm

nodes.statement: $f$ \emph{achieves} its Gauss norm at $t$ if $\lVert a_t \rVert c^t = \lVert f \rVert_c$.
nodes.label: def:achievesgaussnorm

nodes.name: Dominant terms on the antidiagonal
nodes.statement: Let $f, g$ be restricted with nonzero Gauss norms. Fix any well-order on $\sigma$ and let $u$, $w$ be the achieving multidegrees of $f$ and $g$ that are largest for the induced lexicographic order. Then the term $a_u b_w$ strictly dominates every other term of the antidiagonal of $u + w$.
nodes.label: lem:gaussnorm-dominant

nodes.statement: Any other splitting $u' + w' = u + w$ has $u' \neq u$, so by maximality either $u'$ is not achieving --- and then its term is strictly smaller --- or $u'$ is achieving and lexicographically smaller, forcing $w'$ to be lexicographically larger than $w$ and hence non-achieving. Either way one factor is strictly below its Gauss norm.
The Gauss norm is always submultiplicative, and if the norm on $R$ is multiplicative and both series attain their Gauss norms, then \[ \lVert fg \rVert_c = \lVert f \rVert_c \, \lVert g \rVert_c . \]
nodes.label: thm:gaussnorm-mul

nodes.statement: Submultiplicativity is the ultrametric bound on the antidiagonal sum. For equality, the coefficient of $u + w$ from Lemma~\ref{lem:gaussnorm-dominant} is an ultrametric sum with one strictly dominant term, so its norm is $\lVert a_u\rVert \lVert b_w \rVert c^{u+w}$, which is the product of the two Gauss norms.

For strictly positive radii the Gauss norm is a ring norm on $R_c\langle x \rangle$, and it is nonarchimedean whenever the norm on $R$ is. If the norm on $R$ is multiplicative then so is the Gauss norm.
nodes.label: thm:restricted-normedring

nodes.statement: $\lVert a x^t \rVert_c = \lVert a \rVert c^t$, $\lVert C(a) \rVert_c = \lVert a \rVert$ and $\lVert X_i \rVert_c = c_i$; and the norm of a polynomial, viewed in $R_c\langle x\rangle$, is its polynomial Gauss norm --- a finite maximum.
nodes.label: lem:gaussnorm-values

nodes.statement: On polynomials over a field with multiplicative norm the Gauss norm is multiplicative, hence an absolute value. This is Gauss's lemma in its normed form, and the reason the norm carries his name.
nodes.label: prop:polynomial-gaussnorm

nodes.statement: If $R$ is complete then so is $R_c \langle x \rangle$: it is a Banach ring.
nodes.label: thm:restricted-complete

nodes.statement: A Cauchy sequence is coefficientwise Cauchy, since each coefficient functional is norm-nonincreasing, so the coefficients converge in $R$ and assemble into a candidate limit. The point requiring care is that the candidate is itself restricted: the Cauchy estimate is \emph{uniform} in the multidegree, so a tail of the sequence has all its coefficients within $\varepsilon$ of the limit's, and restrictedness of any one member transfers to the limit. Convergence in Gauss norm then follows from the same uniform estimate.
At radius $c = 1$, a restricted power series is power bounded if and only if all its coefficients are, and topologically nilpotent if and only if all its coefficients are.
nodes.label: prop:powerbounded

nodes.statement: Let $R$ be complete. A restricted power series $f$ is a unit if and only if its constant coefficient is a unit of $R$ and every other coefficient is strictly smaller in norm: the Gauss norm is achieved at the constant term alone.
nodes.label: thm:restricted-units

nodes.statement: If $\lVert f - C(f_0)\rVert_c < \lVert f_0 \rVert$ then $f = C(f_0)(1 + \delta)$ with $\lVert \delta \rVert_c < 1$, and $1 + \delta$ is invertible by the geometric series, which converges by Theorem~\ref{thm:restricted-complete}. Conversely if $f$ is a unit then $\lVert f \rVert_c \lVert f^{-1}\rVert_c \geq 1$ forces the norm to be attained at the constant term, and no other coefficient can attain it.

For an ideal $I$ of $R^\circ$ containing the topologically nilpotent elements, reduction gives a surjection $T^\circ \to (R^\circ/I)[x_i]$ onto the \emph{polynomial} ring, whose kernel is the series with all coefficients in $I$. In particular the reduction of a restricted power series is a polynomial.
nodes.label: prop:reduction

nodes.statement: For a polyradius $c$ on $\mathrm{Fin}(n+1)$ there is a ring isomorphism \[ R_c\langle x_0, \dots, x_n \rangle \;\cong\; \bigl(R_{(c_1,\dots,c_n)}\langle x_1, \dots, x_n\rangle\bigr)_{c_0}\!\langle x_0 \rangle, \] and it is an isometry for the Gauss norms.
nodes.label: thm:finsuccequiv

nodes.statement: The underlying bijection regroups the coefficient family, and restrictedness on either side is the same convergence statement grouped differently. The isometry is immediate from Definition~\ref{def:gaussnorm}, since a supremum over pairs is the supremum of the inner suprema.
Over an empty index type the restricted power series are the coefficients themselves, isometrically. This is the base case of the induction.
nodes.label: lem:isemptyequiv

nodes.statement: Let $f \in A_c\langle T \rangle$ and $s \in \N$. We say $f$ is \emph{distinguished of order $s$} if \begin{enumerate} \item $f_s$ is a multiplicative unit of $A$; \item the $s$-th Gauss term attains the Gauss norm, $\lvert f_s \rvert c^s = \lVert f \rVert_c$; and \item it strictly dominates every \emph{later} Gauss term: $\lvert f_i \rvert c^i < \lvert f_s \rvert c^s$ for all $i > s$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.label: def:ismuldistinguished

nodes.name: {\cite[Lemma 1.26]{Martin}}
nodes.statement: Let $g$ be distinguished of order $s$ and let $q \in A_c\langle T\rangle$ be nonzero. Then \[ \lVert g q \rVert_c = \lVert g \rVert_c \lVert q \rVert_c, \] and the product achieves its Gauss norm at the index $s + k_0(q)$, and at no larger index.
nodes.label: lem:martin126

nodes.statement: The coefficient of $T^{s + k_0}$ in $gq$ is $g_s q_{k_0} + \sum_{i + j = s + k_0, \, i \neq s} g_i q_j$. In each remaining term either $i > s$, so that the $i$-th Gauss term of $g$ is strictly dominated by the $s$-th, or $i < s$ and hence $j > k_0$, so that the $j$-th Gauss term of $q$ is strictly dominated by the $k_0$-th by maximality of $k_0$. Either way the term is strictly smaller than $\lvert g_s q_{k_0}\rvert c^{s + k_0}$, which is $\lVert g \rVert_c \lVert q \rVert_c$ because $g_s$ is a multiplicative unit. The ultrametric equality case gives the claim, and the same estimate applied at larger indices gives the maximality.

nodes.name: Weierstrass division, {\cite[Proposition 1.27]{Martin}}
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be complete, $c > 0$, and let $g \in A_c\langle T\rangle$ be distinguished of order $s$. Then every $f \in A_c\langle T \rangle$ can be written \[ f = g q + r, \qquad q \in A_c\langle T\rangle, \quad r \in A[T], \quad \deg r < s, \] and moreover $\lVert f \rVert_c = \max ( \lVert g \rVert_c \lVert q \rVert_c , \lVert r \rVert_c )$.
nodes.label: thm:wdivision

nodes.name: Uniqueness
nodes.statement: The pair $(q, r)$ of Theorem~\ref{thm:wdivision} is unique.
nodes.label: thm:wdivision-unique

nodes.statement: Uniqueness is the norm identity: if $gq + r = gq' + r'$ then $g(q - q') = r' - r$ has degree $< s$, while by Lemma~\ref{lem:martin126} the left-hand side achieves its Gauss norm at an index $\geq s$ unless $q = q'$.

Truncate $g$ to a polynomial $g'$ of degree $s$ agreeing with $g$ up to $T^s$; its leading coefficient $g_s$ is invertible, so Euclidean division in $A[T]$ divides any polynomial by $g'$. Applying this to a polynomial approximation of $f$ produces a one-step approximate division whose error is controlled by the tail factor \[ \theta = \sup_{i > s} \frac{\lvert g_i \rvert c^i}{\lvert g_s \rvert c^s} < 1, \] which is $< 1$ precisely by condition (iii) of Definition~\ref{def:ismuldistinguished}. Iterating contracts the error geometrically; the limit exists by completeness and the bounds of Lemma~\ref{lem:martin126} keep it inside the set of admissible pairs, which is closed.

nodes.name: Weierstrass preparation, {\cite[Corollary 1.28]{Martin}}
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be complete and let $g \in A_c \langle T \rangle$ be distinguished of order $s$. Then \[ g = e \, \omega \] with $\omega \in A[T]$ monic of degree $s$ and $e$ a multiplicative unit of $A_c\langle T \rangle$. The factorisation is unique.
nodes.label: thm:wprep

nodes.statement: Divide $T^s$ by $g$: $T^s = g q + r$ with $\deg r < s$, and set $\omega := T^s - r = gq$. It remains to see that $q$ is a multiplicative unit. By Lemma~\ref{lem:martin126} the product $gq = \omega$ achieves its norm at $s + k_0(q)$, and $\omega$ is monic of degree $s$, forcing $k_0(q) = 0$. Comparing coefficients of $T^s$ gives $1 = \sum_i g_i q_{s - i}$, which exhibits $g_s q_0$ as $1$ minus a strictly smaller quantity, hence a multiplicative unit; and then $q = q_0 (1 + \text{small})$ is a multiplicative unit of $A_c\langle T\rangle$. Uniqueness follows from uniqueness of the division.

Over a complete nontrivially normed field every nonzero element is a multiplicative unit, so Definition~\ref{def:ismuldistinguished} is the classical distinguishedness condition and Theorems~\ref{thm:wdivision} and \ref{thm:wprep} are the classical Weierstrass division and preparation theorems in $K_c\langle T \rangle$, at every radius $c$.
nodes.label: cor:wprep-field

nodes.statement: $f \in R_c\langle X_0, \dots, X_n\rangle$ is \emph{distinguished in $X_0$ of order $s$} if its image under the splitting isomorphism is distinguished of order $s$ in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:ismuldistinguished} over the coefficient ring $R_{(c_1, \dots, c_n)}\langle X_1, \dots, X_n\rangle$.
nodes.label: def:ismuldistinguishedx0

nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a complete ultrametric normed commutative ring, $c$ any polyradius, and $g$ distinguished in $X_0$ of order $s$. Then division by $g$ with remainder of $X_0$-degree $< s$ exists and is unique, and $g$ factors uniquely as $e \omega$ with $\omega$ monic of degree $s$ in $X_0$ over the tail algebra and $e$ a multiplicative unit.
nodes.label: thm:mvweierstrass

nodes.statement: The tail algebra is a complete ultrametric normed commutative ring, so Theorems~\ref{thm:wdivision} and \ref{thm:wprep} apply to it verbatim; transport the conclusions back along the splitting isomorphism.

A \emph{one-sided polygon} over an ordered value group $\Gamma$ consists of a starting vertex in $\Z \times \Gamma$, a sequence of segment lengths, and a monotone sequence of slopes, together with the bookkeeping that says where the polygon stops (it may be finite, may end in a ray, or may continue forever). Monotonicity of the slopes is convexity, built into the structure rather than imposed afterwards.
nodes.label: def:newtonpolygon0

nodes.statement: A one-sided polygon $P$ is \emph{the Newton polygon of} $v$ when \begin{enumerate} \item there are no points of $v$ strictly left of the starting vertex, and the starting vertex is itself a point of $v$; \item $P$ lies on or below every point: $P(k) \leq v_k$ for all $k \in \N$; and \item $P$ is the greatest such: any polygon $Q$ with the same starting abscissa lying on or below every point lies on or below $P$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.label: def:isnewtonpolygonof

nodes.name: Uniqueness
nodes.statement: Two polygons satisfying Definition~\ref{def:isnewtonpolygonof} for the same $v$ have the same height at every integer.
nodes.label: thm:np-unique

nodes.statement: Each is below the other by (iii), applied in both directions.
$v$ is \emph{admissible} if for every finite point of $v$ the set of slopes from that point to later points is bounded below.
nodes.section: 4.2 Existence: the algorithm meets the specification
nodes.label: def:isadmissible

nodes.statement: If the points of $v$ lie on or above a single affine line then $v$ is admissible.
nodes.section: 4.2 Existence: the algorithm meets the specification
nodes.label: lem:isadmissible-affine

nodes.name: Existence
nodes.statement: If $v$ has at least one finite value and is admissible, the polygon $\mathrm{newtonPolygon}_0(v)$ produced by the step algorithm satisfies Definition~\ref{def:isnewtonpolygonof}.
nodes.section: 4.2 Existence: the algorithm meets the specification
nodes.label: thm:np-exists

nodes.statement: For $f = \sum a_i T^i$ over an ultrametric field, $\mathrm{coeffVal}(f)_i = -\log \lVert a_i \rVert$, with the value $\infty$ where $a_i = 0$. The Newton polygon of $f$ is the Newton polygon of this sequence.
nodes.section: 4.3 The polygon of a power series
nodes.label: def:coeffval

nodes.statement: A restricted power series of parameter $c > 0$ has admissible coefficient valuations --- the Gauss bound $\lVert a_k \rVert c^k \leq B$ \emph{is} an affine floor --- hence has a Newton polygon. The same holds for a nonzero polynomial.
nodes.section: 4.3 The polygon of a power series
nodes.label: lem:np-restricted

nodes.statement: For a monotone sequence of reals $s : \N \to \R$ and a starting height $y_0$, let $\mathrm{ofSlopes}(s, y_0)$ be the polygon anchored at $(0, y_0)$ with infinitely many segments of length $1$, the $j$-th having slope $s_j$.
nodes.label: def:ofslopes

nodes.statement: If $v_m = y_0 + \sum_{i < m} s_i$ for every $m$, then $\mathrm{ofSlopes}(s, y_0)$ is the Newton polygon of $v$.
nodes.label: thm:ofslopes

nodes.statement: The polygon passes through every point, so condition (ii) holds with equality; and any competitor lying below the points lies below the polygon at every integer, which is where heights are compared. Admissibility is Lemma~\ref{lem:isadmissible-affine} through the minimum slope $s_0$.
Consequently the polygon built by the algorithm from such a $v$ has unit slopes exactly $s_j$.
nodes.label: cor:ofslopes-transport

nodes.statement: $f$ \emph{has first break $(i, m)$} when the first segment of its polygon has slope $m$ and ends at abscissa $i$. $f$ is \emph{pure of slope $m$} when its polygon is a single segment of slope $m$.
nodes.section: 4.5 First breaks, purity, and the link to preparation
nodes.label: def:hasfirstbreak

nodes.statement: A first break at $(i, m)$ makes $f$ distinguished of order $i$ at the radius $e^{m}$, in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:ismuldistinguished}.
nodes.section: 4.5 First breaks, purity, and the link to preparation
nodes.label: prop:firstbreak-distinguished

nodes.name: Weierstrass factorisation along the polygon
nodes.statement: A power series over a complete field factors, along each break of its polygon, as a polynomial of degree the break abscissa times a unit of the corresponding restricted algebra.
nodes.section: 4.5 First breaks, purity, and the link to preparation
nodes.label: thm:np-factorisation

nodes.statement: A point of the closed disc is a zero of the (convergent) series exactly when it is a root of the polynomial factor supplied by Theorem~\ref{thm:np-factorisation}.
nodes.label: thm:np-zeros

nodes.name: The slope reading
nodes.statement: If $z$ is a zero of $f$ then $\lVert z \rVert = \exp(m)$ for $m$ a slope of the Newton polygon of $f$; and each slope $m$ occurs for exactly as many zeros, with multiplicity, as the horizontal length of the corresponding segment.
nodes.label: thm:np-slope-reading

nodes.statement: The radius of convergence of $f$ is the supremum of the radii at which $f$ is restricted, and $f$ is restricted at every smaller radius. In polygon terms it is $\exp$ of the supremum of the slopes.
nodes.label: prop:np-radius

nodes.statement: A polygon has \emph{unbounded slopes} if every real number is exceeded by one of its unit slopes, the junk value $\infty$ past a finite polygon counting. Polynomials qualify through that junk tail, and entire series because their coefficients lie above a line of every slope.
nodes.label: def:slopesunbounded

nodes.statement: For a real $\sigma$, $\mathrm{faceLeft}(\sigma)$ is the number of unit slopes strictly below $\sigma$ and $\mathrm{faceRight}(\sigma)$ the number at most $\sigma$. These are the two endpoints of the face of slope $\sigma$; the polygon is the line of slope $\sigma$ between them and strictly above it outside.
nodes.label: def:face

nodes.statement: Where the unit slope strictly increases, the polygon meets the point sequence. In particular both endpoints of every face are points. (Textbooks take this as the definition of a vertex; against the specification it is a theorem, proved by raising a supporting line of an intermediate slope and contradicting maximality.)
nodes.label: prop:vertex-is-point

nodes.statement: The height at $n$ of the Minkowski sum of two polygons is $\min_{i + j = n}\bigl(P(i) + Q(j)\bigr)$, the infimal convolution of the two height functions.
nodes.label: def:minkowskiheight

nodes.name: The polygon of a product
nodes.statement: For $f$ and $g$ with nonzero constant coefficient and unbounded slopes, the Newton polygon of $fg$ is the Minkowski sum of the polygons of $f$ and $g$.
nodes.label: thm:np-product

nodes.statement: Both inequalities come from the face of a common slope. The ultrametric bound puts every point of $fg$ on or above the Minkowski sum, since $c_n = \sum_{i+j=n} a_i b_j$. A minimising split of $n$ admits a slope $\sigma$ supporting both factors there, so the sum of the two supporting lines lies below every point of $fg$ and hence below its polygon; that is one inequality. For the other, at the two endpoints of the face of slope $\sigma$ the minimising split is \emph{unique}, so the ultrametric bound is an equality there and the endpoints are genuine points of $fg$. The polygon of $fg$ is therefore below the chord joining them, and that chord is exactly the Minkowski sum on the face.

nodes.name: Multiplicities add
nodes.statement: The number of slopes of $fg$ that are at most $\sigma$ is the sum of the corresponding counts for $f$ and for $g$; likewise for the slopes strictly below $\sigma$. Equivalently, the slope multiset of $fg$ is the union of the slope multisets of $f$ and $g$.
nodes.label: cor:np-product-multiplicity

nodes.name: The initial segment
nodes.statement: If the first $n$ slopes of $g$ are at most every slope of $f$, then the polygon of $fg$ agrees with that of $g$ up to $n$. Applied to a Fredholm determinant factored as a polynomial times the determinant of the complement, this says the finite factor supplies the initial segment of the polygon --- the form used in Chapter~\ref{chap:slopes}.
nodes.label: cor:np-product-initial

nodes.statement: A \emph{Banach--Tate ring} is a complete normed ring $R$ possessing a \emph{pseudo-uniformizer}: a unit $\varpi$ with $\lVert \varpi \rVert < 1$ whose norm is multiplicative. We write $\mathrm{IsTate}\, R$.
nodes.label: def:istate

nodes.statement: For an index type $I$ the \emph{model space} $c(I, R)$ is the space of families $(x_i)_{i \in I}$ in $R$ tending to $0$ along the cofinite filter, with the supremum norm.
nodes.label: def:cspace

nodes.statement: A Banach $R$-module $M$ is \emph{orthonormalisable} if it is isometrically isomorphic to some $c(I,R)$, and has \emph{property (Pr)} if it is a direct summand of an orthonormalisable module.
nodes.label: def:onable

nodes.statement: The Tate algebra $K\langle X \rangle$ is orthonormalisable, with the monomials $X^n$ as orthonormal basis; the isometry $K\langle X\rangle \cong c(\N, K)$ sends a series to its coefficient family.
nodes.label: prop:tate-algebra-onable

nodes.statement: For $u : c(I,R) \to c(J,R)$ continuous linear, the \emph{matrix coefficient} $u_{j i}$ is the $j$-th coordinate of $u(e_i)$, where $e_i$ is the $i$-th basis vector. The $j$-th \emph{row norm} is $\sup_i \lVert u_{ji}\rVert$.
nodes.label: def:matrixcoeff

nodes.statement: $u$ is \emph{completely continuous} if it is an operator-norm limit of finite-rank operators, and \emph{compactoid} if its row norms tend to $0$ along the cofinite filter.
nodes.label: def:iscompactoid

nodes.statement: On $c(I,R)$ the two notions agree, and a row-decay estimate $\lVert u_{ji} \rVert \leq C \sigma^{j}$ with $\sigma < 1$ suffices for both.
nodes.label: prop:compactoid-criterion

nodes.statement: For a finite $S \subseteq I$ let $\mathrm{minor}(u, S)$ be the determinant of the $S \times S$ submatrix of $u$. For compactoid $u$ the family of $n$-element minors is summable, and \[ c_n(u) = (-1)^n \sum_{\lvert S \rvert = n} \mathrm{minor}(u, S), \qquad \det(1 - Tu) = \sum_{n \geq 0} c_n(u) T^n . \]
nodes.label: def:minor

nodes.name: Ultrametric Hadamard bound
nodes.statement: If every entry of a square matrix satisfies $\lVert A_{ji}\rVert \leq \sigma^{w_j}$ for a row weight $w$, then $\lVert \det A \rVert \leq \sigma^{\sum_j w_j}$.
nodes.label: lem:hadamard

nodes.statement: Each Leibniz monomial picks one entry from every row, so has norm at most $\prod_j \sigma^{w_j}$; the ultrametric inequality bounds the sum of the monomials by their maximum.
For compactoid $u$ the series $\det(1 - Tu)$ is entire, with constant term $1$.
nodes.label: thm:charpowerseries-entire

nodes.name: Invariances
nodes.statement: $\det(1 - Tuv) = \det(1 - Tvu)$, and the determinant is invariant under conjugation by an isomorphism. Consequently it may be computed in any model of the space.
nodes.label: thm:charpowerseries-inv

nodes.name: Block operators
nodes.statement: An operator on $c(\sigma \times I, R)$ with $\sigma$ finite is assembled from its $\sigma \times \sigma$ blocks; it is compactoid iff each block is, and its determinant is computed blockwise.
nodes.label: prop:blockop

nodes.name: {\cite[Prop.\ 11]{Serre}}
nodes.statement: For compactoid $u$ and $a \in R$, the operator $1 - a u$ is invertible if and only if $\det(1-Tu)$ evaluated at $a$ is a unit.
nodes.label: thm:serre11

nodes.name: {\cite[Prop.\ 12]{Serre}}
nodes.statement: Over a field, if $a \neq 0$ is a zero of $\det(1 - Tu)$ then $a^{-1}$ is an eigenvalue of $u$; and conversely.
nodes.label: thm:serre12

nodes.name: Riesz decomposition
nodes.statement: Let $u$ be compactoid on $c(I,K)$ over a discretely valued complete field, and let $a$ be a zero of $\det(1 - Tu)$ of multiplicity $h$. Then $c(I,K) = N \oplus F$ with both summands $u$-stable, $(1 - au)^h$ vanishing on $N$, $(1-au)$ invertible on $F$, and \[ \dim_K N = h . \]
nodes.label: thm:riesz

nodes.statement: Write $D_f = D \otimes_F \A_F^\infty$ and $D_f^\times$ for its unit group. The subgroup $\Gamma = \mathrm{globalUnits}$ is the image of $D^\times$ in $D_f^\times$.
nodes.label: def:dfx

nodes.statement: A \emph{rigidification at $v$} is a fixed isomorphism $D \otimes_F F_v \cong M_2(F_v)$; it exists exactly when $D$ splits at $v$. Composing the local component map $\mathrm{toLocal}_v : D_f \to D \otimes_F F_v$ with it gives $\mathrm{toMatrix}_v : D_f^\times \to M_2(F_v)$.
nodes.label: def:rigidification

nodes.statement: For $\gamma < 1$ in the value group let \[ \Sigma_0(\gamma) = \left\{ g = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d\end{pmatrix} \in M_2(F_v) \;:\; v(g_{ij}) \leq 1, \; v(c) \leq \gamma, \; v(d) = 1, \; \det g \neq 0 \right\}, \] the matrices that are integral, congruent to upper-triangular modulo $\gamma$, and with unit lower-right entry. A subgroup $U \subseteq D_f^\times$ has \emph{wild level $\geq \gamma$} if $\mathrm{toMatrix}_v(U) \subseteq \Sigma_0(\gamma)$; this is Buzzard's condition \cite[\S9]{Buzzard}, and $\Delta = \mathrm{toMatrix}_v^{-1}(\Sigma_0(\gamma))$ is the monoid on which the weight will act.
nodes.label: def:sigma0

nodes.statement: $\mathrm{LevelBounds}\, S\, \rho$ records the norm estimates extracted from an acting monoid $S$: entries integral, $\lVert c \rVert \leq \rho$, and $\lVert d \rVert = 1$.
nodes.label: def:levelbounds

nodes.statement: A \emph{weight datum} $W$ at $(S, \rho)$ consists of the level bounds, the expansion $\kappa\mathrm{col}(c,d) \in K[[z]]$ of $\kappa(cz+d)$ as a function of the lower row, the decay estimate $\lVert \mathrm{coeff}_m \rVert \leq \rho^m$, absolute summability, and the cocycle identity making $\|_\kappa$ an action.
nodes.label: def:weightseries

nodes.statement: An \emph{analytic weight} is a genuine character $\kappa : U_K \to K^\times$ together with an expansion datum for it. The expansion is unique on the level, so the pair is no more data than the character; but carrying it makes the weight action a definition rather than a choice.
nodes.label: def:analyticweight

nodes.statement: $\kappa\text{-}\mathrm{slash}(g)$ is the continuous $K$-linear operator on the Tate algebra determined by $z^k \mapsto \kappa(cz+d)(cz+d)^{-2}\left(\frac{az+b}{cz+d}\right)^k$.
nodes.label: def:kappaslash

nodes.statement: Under the identification of Proposition~\ref{prop:tate-algebra-onable}, the matrix of $\kappa\text{-}\mathrm{slash}(g)$ is the coefficient array of the two-variable generating function $\kappa\mathrm{col}\cdot(cx+d)^{-1}(cx+d-axy-by)^{-1}$; and if $\lVert a \rVert \leq \sigma$ with $\rho \leq \sigma$ then \[ \lVert \mathrm{matrixCoeff}(\kappa\text{-}\mathrm{slash}(g))_{j i} \rVert \leq \sigma^{\,j}. \]
nodes.label: prop:kappaslash-matrix

nodes.statement: Let $\theta$ be the component map, $S$ an acting monoid, $\kappa$ an analytic weight, $U$ a subgroup with $\theta(U) \subseteq S$, and $\chi$ a twisting character. Then \[ S_\kappa(U) = \left\{ \varphi : D_f^\times \to K\langle z\rangle \;:\; \varphi(dgu) = \chi(u_v)\, \varphi(g) \|_\kappa u_v \ \ \forall d \in \Gamma,\ u \in U \right\}. \]
nodes.label: def:forms

nodes.statement: For $\eta$ in the acting monoid, write $U \eta U = \coprod_i U x_i$ and set $[U\eta U]\varphi = \sum_i \varphi \|_\kappa x_i$. This is independent of the representatives and preserves $S_\kappa(U)$.
nodes.label: def:heckeoperator

nodes.statement: If $U$ is open and compact then $U \eta U$ is a finite union of right cosets of $U$.
nodes.label: thm:hecke-finiteness

nodes.statement: The standard levels are compact open. Concretely: the units of a compact multiplicatively closed set form a compact set of units, because $u \mapsto (u, u^{-1})$ is a closed embedding; and the integral order $\calO_D \otimes \Zhat \subseteq D_f$ is compact, being the image of a product of compact local integer rings under a continuous coordinate map.
nodes.label: prop:compact-open-levels

nodes.name: Fujisaki
nodes.statement: For $U$ open the class set $\Gamma \backslash D_f^\times / U$ is finite.
nodes.label: thm:fujisaki

nodes.statement: $\mathrm{evalAtReps}(\varphi) = (\varphi(c_i))_i$, a map $S_\kappa(U) \to c(\iota \times \N, K)$.
nodes.label: def:evalatreps

nodes.statement: $\mathrm{evalAtReps}$ is injective, and its image is exactly the tuples whose $i$-th block is $\Gamma_i$-invariant. If the level is \emph{neat} --- every $\Gamma_i$ acts trivially on the Tate algebra --- it is bijective, so $S_\kappa(U) \cong c(\iota \times \N, K)$.
nodes.label: thm:evalatreps

nodes.statement: Given right coset representatives $v_t$ of $U\eta U$ and, for each $(i,t)$, a factorisation $c_i v_t^{-1} = d_{i,t}\, c_{\sigma(i,t)}\, u_{i,t}$ with $d_{i,t} \in \Gamma$, $u_{i,t} \in U$, the $(i,j)$ \emph{block} is \[ \varepsilon_{ij} = \sum_{t \,:\, \sigma(i,t) = j} \chi(w_{i,t})\, \kappa\text{-}\mathrm{slash}(w_{i,t}), \qquad w_{i,t} = \theta(u_{i,t} v_t), \] and $\mathrm{heckeBlockOp}$ is the operator on $c(\iota \times \N, K)$ they assemble.
nodes.label: def:heckeblock

nodes.name: The transport
nodes.statement: $\bigl([U\eta U]\varphi\bigr)(c_i) = \sum_j \varepsilon_{ij}\bigl(\varphi(c_j)\bigr)$; that is, $\mathrm{evalAtReps}$ intertwines $[U\eta U]$ with $\mathrm{heckeBlockOp}$.
nodes.label: thm:transport

nodes.name: {\cite[Lemma 12.2]{Buzzard}}, {[Jacobs, Lemma 2.7]}
nodes.statement: Suppose $\lVert \det \theta(\eta) \rVert \leq \sigma$ with $\rho \leq \sigma < 1$. Then every block, and hence the block operator, is compactoid.
nodes.label: thm:qmf-compact

nodes.statement: Each certificate element $u_{i,t}v_t$ has determinant norm at most that of $\eta$, the outer factors being integral; a small determinant with integral entries and unit $d$ forces $\lVert a \rVert \leq \sigma$; and then Proposition~\ref{prop:kappaslash-matrix} gives the row decay $\sigma^j$, which is Proposition~\ref{prop:compactoid-criterion}'s hypothesis. A finite sum of compactoid operators is compactoid.
$\det(1 - T\,[U\eta U])$, computed in the block model.
nodes.label: def:heckecharpowerseries

nodes.name: Eigenforms are reciprocal roots
nodes.statement: At a neat level, $a \neq 0$ is a zero of $\det(1 - T[U\eta U])$ if and only if $a^{-1}$ is an eigenvalue of $[U\eta U]$ on $S_\kappa(U)$.
nodes.label: thm:qmf-eigenform-criterion

nodes.statement: Each zero $a$ of the determinant, of multiplicity $n$, gives a decomposition $S_\kappa(U) = N \oplus F$ into $[U\eta U]$-stable summands with $(1 - a[U\eta U])^n = 0$ on $N$, invertible on $F$, and $\dim_K N = n$.
nodes.label: thm:qmf-riesz

nodes.statement: Without neatness, averaging over the finite stabilisers gives projectors realising $S_\kappa(U)$ as a direct summand of the model, so it satisfies property (Pr). The determinant of $[U\eta U]$ on the summand is well defined and independent of the projector chosen \cite[Lemma 2.12]{Buzzard}.
nodes.label: prop:pr

nodes.statement: If $\kappa'$ over $L$ is compatible with $\kappa$ over $K$ along an isometric embedding $K \to L$, then the two determinants correspond \cite[Lemma 2.13]{Buzzard}. This is what lets a computation made over a small field be read over $\bbC_p$.
nodes.section: 6.7 Base change and the Hecke algebra
nodes.label: prop:qmf-basechange

nodes.statement: Two double coset operators commute as soon as their representative families can be matched pairwise, up to the level, with the two products taken in the opposite orders.
nodes.section: 6.7 Base change and the Hecke algebra
nodes.label: prop:hecke-comm-criterion

nodes.statement: Let $\mathbb{T}$ be a commuting family of endomorphisms of $S_\kappa(U)$, each commuting with $\varphi = [U\eta U]$, and let $N$ be the finite-slope subspace of Theorem~\ref{thm:qmf-riesz}. Then every element of $\mathbb{T}$ preserves $N$, and over an algebraically closed coefficient field $N$ contains a nonzero simultaneous generalised eigenvector: a $\varphi$-finite system of eigenvalues.
nodes.section: 6.7 Base change and the Hecke algebra
nodes.label: prop:qmf-eigensystem

nodes.statement: Stability is the identity $(1-a\varphi)^n t = t (1-a\varphi)^n$ applied to a vector killed by the left factor. $N$ is finite dimensional by Theorem~\ref{thm:qmf-riesz} and nonzero, and a commuting family of endomorphisms of a nonzero finite-dimensional space over an algebraically closed field is simultaneously triangularisable.
nodes.section: 6.7 Base change and the Hecke algebra

nodes.statement: If $\lVert u_{ji}\rVert \leq \sigma^{w_j}$ for all $i, j$ then $\lVert \mathrm{minor}(u, S) \rVert \leq \sigma^{\sum_{j \in S} w_j}$ for every finite $S$.
nodes.section: 7.1 From row decay to coefficient bounds
nodes.label: lem:minor-bound

nodes.name: The slope bound
nodes.statement: Let $0 \leq \sigma < 1$, let $u$ be compactoid with $\lVert u_{ji}\rVert \leq \sigma^{w_j}$, and let $f : \N \to \N$ satisfy $f(n) \leq \sum_{j \in S} w_j$ for every $S$ with $\lvert S \rvert = n$. Then \[ \lVert c_n(u) \rVert \leq \sigma^{f(n)} . \]
nodes.section: 7.1 From row decay to coefficient bounds
nodes.label: thm:slope-bound

nodes.statement: $c_n$ is $\pm$ the sum of the $n$-element minors, and an ultrametric infinite sum is bounded by the supremum of its terms; each term is bounded by Lemma~\ref{lem:minor-bound} and then by $\sigma^{f(n)}$ since $\sigma \leq 1$ and $f(n)$ is the smaller exponent.
nodes.section: 7.1 From row decay to coefficient bounds

nodes.statement: Among $n$-element subsets of $\N$, the sum $\sum_{i \in S} i$ is minimised uniquely by $S = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$, with value $\binom{n}{2}$; every other $n$-element subset has sum at least $\binom{n}{2} + 1$.
nodes.section: 7.1 From row decay to coefficient bounds
nodes.label: lem:choose-two

nodes.statement: On $\iota \times \N$ with $\lvert \iota \rvert = d$ and weight $(i, m) \mapsto m$, an $n$-element subset has weight sum at least $\sum_{k < n} \lfloor k/d \rfloor$: each value of $m$ can be used at most $d$ times.
nodes.section: 7.1 From row decay to coefficient bounds
nodes.label: lem:block-weight

nodes.statement: Peel off an element $M$ of maximal second coordinate. Since $S \subseteq \iota \times \{0, \dots, M_2\}$, which has $d(M_2+1)$ elements, we get $n \leq d(M_2+1)$ and hence $\lfloor (n-1)/d\rfloor \leq M_2$. Induct on the remaining $n-1$ elements.
nodes.section: 7.1 From row decay to coefficient bounds

nodes.statement: On $c(\N, K)$ with $\lVert u_{ji}\rVert \leq \sigma^j$ we get $\lVert c_n \rVert \leq \sigma^{\binom{n}{2}}$; on the block model $c(\iota \times \N, K)$ we get $\lVert c_n \rVert \leq \sigma^{\sum_{k<n} \lfloor k/\lvert\iota\rvert\rfloor}$.
nodes.section: 7.1 From row decay to coefficient bounds
nodes.label: cor:slope-bound-block

nodes.statement: With $\lVert \det\theta(\eta)\rVert \leq \sigma$, $\rho \leq \sigma$, and a twisting character of norm at most $1$, the block operator satisfies $\lVert \mathrm{matrixCoeff}_{(i,m),(j,r)} \rVert \leq \sigma^{m}$.
nodes.section: 7.2 The slope theorem at a general weight
nodes.label: prop:qmf-row-decay

nodes.statement: The coefficients of $\det(1 - T[U\eta U])$ satisfy \[ \lVert c_n \rVert \leq \sigma^{\sum_{k < n}\lfloor k/\lvert \iota\rvert\rfloor}. \]
nodes.section: 7.2 The slope theorem at a general weight
nodes.label: thm:qmf-slope-bound

nodes.statement: The \emph{block slope sequence} is $s_k = \lfloor k/d \rfloor \cdot (-\log \sigma)$, where $d = \lvert \iota \rvert$ is the size of the class set: each of the values $0, -\log\sigma, -2\log\sigma, \dots$ repeated $d$ times, once per block. It is monotone since $\sigma < 1$.
nodes.section: 7.2 The slope theorem at a general weight
nodes.label: def:blockslopes

nodes.name: The slope theorem at a general analytic weight
nodes.statement: The Newton polygon of $\det(1 - T[U\eta U])$ lies on or above the polygon anchored at the origin whose $k$-th unit slope is $\lfloor k/\lvert\iota\rvert\rfloor \cdot (-\log \sigma)$.
nodes.section: 7.2 The slope theorem at a general weight
nodes.label: thm:qmf-slope-theorem

nodes.statement: The determinant has constant coefficient $1$, so its polygon is anchored at the origin, and all its coefficients have norm at most $1$, which is an affine floor and hence admissibility. The comparison polygon is $\mathrm{ofSlopes}$ of the block slope sequence, whose height at $k$ is $\sum_{i<k} s_i$; the required inequality height $\leq -\log\lVert c_k\rVert$ is Theorem~\ref{thm:qmf-slope-bound} after taking logarithms. Now apply the maximality clause of Definition~\ref{def:isnewtonpolygonof}.
nodes.section: 7.2 The slope theorem at a general weight

nodes.name: {[Jacobs, Theorem 2.12]}
nodes.statement: Let $u$ on $c(\N,K)$ satisfy $\lVert u_{ji}\rVert \leq \lVert \varpi \rVert^j$ and suppose the rescaled matrix $N_{ji} = \varpi^{-j} u_{ji}$ has every top-left minor of norm $1$. Then \[ \lVert c_m(u) \rVert = \lVert \varpi \rVert^{\binom{m}{2}} \qquad \text{exactly}. \]
nodes.label: thm:unit-minors

nodes.statement: The principal block $S = \{0,\dots,m-1\}$ contributes exactly $\lVert\varpi\rVert^{\binom m2}$: factoring $\varpi^j$ out of the $j$-th row leaves the unit-minor matrix. Every other $m$-element block contributes strictly less, since its row sum exceeds $\binom m2$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:choose-two}. An ultrametric sum with one strictly dominant term has the norm of that term.

nodes.name: The slope reading
nodes.statement: Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:unit-minors} the Newton polygon of $\det(1-Tu)$, in the normalisation $v(\varpi) = 1$, has unit slopes $0, 1, 2, 3, \dots$. Consequently the eigenvalues of $u$ have valuations $0, 1, 2, \dots$: an arithmetic progression.
nodes.label: cor:slope-reading

nodes.statement: The valuations $v(c_m) = \binom m2$ are the partial sums of $0,1,2,\dots$, so Theorem~\ref{thm:ofslopes} identifies the polygon and Corollary~\ref{cor:ofslopes-transport} reads its slopes. Passing to eigenvalues is Theorem~\ref{thm:np-slope-reading} together with Theorem~\ref{thm:serre12}.

Let $D = \bbH_{\Q}$ be Hamilton's quaternions over $\Q$, a definite quaternion algebra of discriminant $2$; let $v_3$ be the place above $3$ and $K_3 = \Q_3$ its completion. Since $3 \nmid 2$, $D$ splits at $v_3$, and a splitting is fixed by choosing a square root $\nu$ of $-2$ in $K_3$; the resulting isomorphism $\theta_3 : D \otimes_{\Q} K_3 \cong M_2(K_3)$ is the rigidification of Definition~\ref{def:rigidification}.
nodes.label: def:jacobs-setting

nodes.statement: The \emph{Hurwitz order} is $\calO = \Z\langle i, j, \tfrac12(1+i+j+k)\rangle \subseteq \bbH_{\Q}$, the unique maximal order up to conjugacy. We record membership by the parity condition that $2x$ has integer coordinates all of the same parity.
nodes.label: def:hurwitz

nodes.statement: A Hurwitz quaternion is a unit exactly when its reduced norm is $1$, and $\calO^\times$ has exactly $24$ elements.
nodes.label: prop:hurwitz-units

nodes.statement: $U_0(1) \subseteq D_f^\times$ consists of the adelic units integral at every finite place --- the unit group of $\calO \otimes \Zhat$ --- and $U_1(9)$ refines it by the congruence $\theta_3(g) \equiv \left(\begin{smallmatrix} * & * \\ 0 & 1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ modulo $9$.
nodes.label: def:jacobs-levels

nodes.statement: $U_0(1)$ and $U_1(9)$ are compact open, so Theorem~\ref{thm:hecke-finiteness} applies and the Hecke operators at this level are defined without exhibiting representatives.
nodes.label: prop:jacobs-levels-compact-open

nodes.statement: The everywhere-integral elements of $D \otimes \A_f$ are exactly the $\Zhat$-span of the Hurwitz basis $1, i, j, \omega$: one inclusion is clear, and the other extracts each coordinate by a $\Q$-linear functional, extends it to the completion, and uses that a rational integral at every finite place is a rational integer. That set is compact by Proposition~\ref{prop:compact-open-levels} and open because the integral adeles are open, so $U_0(1)$ is compact open; $U_1(9)$ is cut out of it by a congruence condition at $3$, which is clopen because closed balls in an ultrametric field are open.

nodes.name: {[Jacobs, Theorem 2.1]}
nodes.statement: $D_f^\times = D^\times \cdot U_0(1)$, and the class set at level $U_1(9)$ has exactly three elements, represented by explicit adelic $c_0, c_1, c_2$.
nodes.label: thm:jacobs-classset

nodes.statement: Class number one for the Hurwitz order is classical; formalised here by the idelic dictionary, reducing a global integrality statement to local approximation. Passing from $U_0(1)$ to $U_1(9)$ replaces the class set by the orbits of $\calO^\times$ on the primitive vectors of $(\Z/9)^2$, which are computed to be three.

nodes.name: {[Jacobs, Lemma 2.2]}
nodes.statement: The stabilisers $\Gamma_i = c_i^{-1}D^\times c_i \cap U_1(9)$ are trivial.
nodes.label: lem:jacobs-neat

nodes.statement: For $t \in K_3$ with $\lVert t \rVert < 1$ let $\kappa_t(u) = u^t := \exp(t \log u)$ on the $1$-units. The expansion of $\kappa_t(cz+d)$ is the binomial series, whose coefficients satisfy the decay required by Definition~\ref{def:weightseries}; the pair is an analytic weight in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:analyticweight}.
nodes.label: def:jacobs-weight

nodes.statement: $U_3 = [U_1(9)\, \eta_3\, U_1(9)]$ where $\eta_3$ is the adelic element which is $1$ away from $3$ and $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\0&3\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ at $3$.
nodes.label: def:u3

nodes.statement: With respect to the three representatives, $(U_3\varphi)(c_i) = \sum_j \varepsilon_{ij} (\varphi(c_j))$, and the matrix coefficients of the blocks $\varepsilon_{ij}$ are the explicit coefficients of the generating functions of Proposition~\ref{prop:kappaslash-matrix} evaluated at the certificate elements.
nodes.label: thm:u3-matrix

nodes.statement: $\det(1 - T\,U_3)$, computed in the block model through the three evaluations.
nodes.label: def:u3-det

nodes.statement: Over an isometric extension containing $\omega$, $\det(1 - TU_3)$ factors according to the $\omega$-eigenspaces of the block structure, and on the relevant factor the rescaled matrix has every top-left minor of norm $1$.
nodes.label: thm:u3-factorisation

nodes.name: The crux
nodes.statement: For every $j \in \N$ there is an eigenvalue $a$ of $U_3$ with \[ v_3(a) = j + \tfrac12 . \]
nodes.label: thm:u3-eigenvalues

nodes.statement: Theorem~\ref{thm:u3-factorisation} puts the relevant factor in the shape of Theorem~\ref{thm:unit-minors} with $\varpi = \sqrt{-3}$, whose valuation is $\tfrac12$ in the normalisation $v_3(3) = 1$. The exact coefficient valuations $\binom m2$ in that normalisation become $\tfrac12\binom m2$ here, whose successive differences are $\tfrac12, \tfrac32, \dots$; Corollary~\ref{cor:slope-reading} reads these off the polygon and Theorem~\ref{thm:serre12} converts slopes into eigenvalues.

nodes.name: The crux, for forms
nodes.statement: For every $j \in \N$ there exist $a \in \bbC_3$ and a nonzero overconvergent quaternionic modular form $\varphi$ of weight $\kappa_t$ and level $U_1(9)$ over $\bbC_3$ with \[ U_3 \varphi = a\varphi, \qquad v_3(a) = j + \tfrac12 . \]
nodes.label: thm:u3-eigenforms

nodes.statement: Theorem~\ref{thm:u3-eigenvalues} produces an eigenvector in the block model; the level is neat by Lemma~\ref{lem:jacobs-neat}, so Theorem~\ref{thm:evalatreps} transports it back to a form, and the transport intertwines the block operator with $U_3$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:transport}. Base change along $K_3(\omega) \hookrightarrow \bbC_3$ is Proposition~\ref{prop:qmf-basechange}.

A power series $F = \sum a_n T^n$ over a normed ring $R$ is \emph{entire} if $\lVert a_n\rVert C^n \to 0$ for every $C > 0$; equivalently, if it is restricted at every radius in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:isrestricted}. The entire series form a subring $R\{\{T\}\}$ of $R\llbracket T\rrbracket$. A \emph{Fredholm series} is an entire series with constant term $1$.
nodes.label: def:isentire

nodes.name: Euclidean division in $R\{\{T\}\}$, {\cite[Proposition II.2.8]{Bellaiche}}
nodes.statement: Let $g \in R[T]$ have invertible leading coefficient and degree $n$. Every entire $F$ can be written uniquely as $F = g\,q + r$ with $q$ entire and $r$ a polynomial of degree $< n$.
nodes.label: thm:entire-division

nodes.statement: Existence and uniqueness are Martin's Weierstrass division (Theorem~\ref{thm:wdivision} and Theorem~\ref{thm:wdivision-unique}) applied at a radius large enough that $g$ dominates: the divisor of a distinguished division is precisely a polynomial whose leading coefficient achieves the Gauss norm, and for a polynomial with invertible leading coefficient this happens at all sufficiently large radii. Entireness of the quotient is then the statement that the division is performed at every radius simultaneously, which uniqueness supplies.
Two entire series are \emph{relatively prime in $R\{\{T\}\}$} if the ideal they generate is the unit ideal (\cite[Definition 2.2.1]{JN}).
nodes.label: def:isentirecoprime

nodes.name: {\cite[Corollary II.2.9]{Bellaiche}}
nodes.statement: If $F = g\,q + r$ is the division of Theorem~\ref{thm:entire-division}, then $F$ and $g$ are relatively prime in $R\{\{T\}\}$ if and only if $r$ and $g$ are relatively prime in $R[T]$.
nodes.label: lem:coprime-remainder

nodes.statement: An entire $F$ has a \emph{good zero of order $s$} at $a$ if the divided derivatives $\Delta^{i}F$ vanish at $a$ for $i < s$ and $\Delta^{s}F(a)$ is a unit (\cite[Definition II.2.11]{Bellaiche}). The divided derivatives obey the Leibniz rule $\Delta^{s}(FG) = \sum_{i+j=s}\Delta^{i}F\cdot\Delta^{j}G$, so good zeros multiply.
nodes.label: def:isgoodzero

nodes.statement: For polynomials $B, P$ over a commutative ring and $N \geq \deg P$, set \[ D_N(B,P) \;=\; \Res_X\bigl(P^{*}, \; 1 - T\,B(X)\bigr) \in R[T], \] the resultant of the reversed polynomial $P^{*} = \mathrm{reflect}_N P$ against $1 - T B(X)$. We also write $b_Q = 1 - u^{-1}Q^{*}$ for a polynomial $Q$ with leading coefficient the unit $u$; this is Bella\"iche's auxiliary polynomial.
nodes.section: 9.2 Coleman's $D(B,P)$ and the spectral mapping formula
nodes.label: def:dpoly

nodes.name: {\cite[Lemma II.2.13]{Bellaiche}}
nodes.statement: $D_N(B, PQ) = D_N(B,P)\,D_N(B,Q)$: the construction is multiplicative in its second argument.
nodes.section: 9.2 Coleman's $D(B,P)$ and the spectral mapping formula
nodes.label: lem:dpoly-mul

nodes.statement: Multiplicativity of the resultant in its first argument, together with $\mathrm{reflect}(PQ) = \mathrm{reflect}(P)\,\mathrm{reflect}(Q)$ at compatible degrees.
nodes.section: 9.2 Coleman's $D(B,P)$ and the spectral mapping formula

nodes.name: The finite-dimensional case
nodes.statement: For a square matrix $A$ over any commutative ring and any polynomial $g$, \[ \Res(\mathrm{charpoly}\,A,\; g) \;=\; \det\bigl(g(A)\bigr). \]
nodes.section: 9.2 Coleman's $D(B,P)$ and the spectral mapping formula
nodes.label: prop:resultant-charpoly

nodes.statement: Over an algebraically closed field both sides equal $\prod_\lambda g(\lambda)$ over the eigenvalues with multiplicity. The general case follows from the universal characteristic polynomial: both sides are polynomial identities in the matrix entries and the coefficients of $g$, so it suffices to verify them over $\Z[x_{ij}, y_k]$, which embeds in an algebraic closure of its fraction field.
nodes.section: 9.2 Coleman's $D(B,P)$ and the spectral mapping formula

nodes.statement: For a Fredholm series $F$ over a Banach--Tate ring, $D(B,F)$ is the coefficientwise limit of $D_N(B, \mathrm{trunc}_N F)$. The limit exists because each coefficient of $D_N$ is a fixed polynomial in the coefficients of the truncation, and that polynomial is Lipschitz in them; $D(B, \cdot)$ is multiplicative and carries entire series to entire series.
nodes.section: 9.2 Coleman's $D(B,P)$ and the spectral mapping formula
nodes.label: def:dseries

nodes.name: {\cite[Lemma II.2.14 and Proposition II.2.15]{Bellaiche}}
nodes.statement: Let $Q$ be a polynomial with unit leading coefficient and constant term $1$, and $S$ a Fredholm series. Then $D(b_Q, S)(1)$ is a unit if and only if $Q$ and $S$ are relatively prime in $R\{\{T\}\}$; and $D(b_Q, QS)$ has a good zero of order $\deg Q$ at $1$.
nodes.section: 9.2 Coleman's $D(B,P)$ and the spectral mapping formula
nodes.label: lem:dseries-goodzero

nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:dpoly-mul}, $D(b_Q, QS) = D(b_Q, Q)\,D(b_Q, S)$. The first factor is computed directly: $b_Q$ was built so that $D(b_Q, Q)$ is $(1-T)^{\deg Q}$ up to a unit, which is a good zero of order $\deg Q$ at $1$. The second factor is a unit at $1$ by the coprimality criterion, which is Lemma~\ref{lem:coprime-remainder} transported through the resultant. Good zeros multiply by the Leibniz rule of Definition~\ref{def:isgoodzero}.
nodes.section: 9.2 Coleman's $D(B,P)$ and the spectral mapping formula

nodes.name: Spectral mapping, {\cite[Proposition II.2.16]{Bellaiche}}
nodes.statement: For a compactoid $\varphi$ on $c(I,R)$ and any polynomial $B$ with $B(0)=0$, \[ \det\bigl(1 - T\,B(\varphi)\bigr) \;=\; D\bigl(B, \det(1-T\varphi)\bigr). \]
nodes.section: 9.2 Coleman's $D(B,P)$ and the spectral mapping formula
nodes.label: thm:spectral-mapping

nodes.statement: For a finite matrix this is Proposition~\ref{prop:resultant-charpoly} rewritten in reversed form. A compactoid operator is a limit of its truncations to finite blocks, both sides are continuous in the operator coefficientwise, and $D(B,\cdot)$ was defined as exactly that limit.
nodes.section: 9.2 Coleman's $D(B,P)$ and the spectral mapping formula

nodes.name:
{\cite[Theorem 2.2.2]{JN}; \cite[Theorem 3.3]{Buzzard};
                 \cite[Theorem A4.3]{Coleman}}
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a Banach--Tate ring, $u$ compactoid on $M = c(I,R)$, and suppose $\det(1-Tu) = Q\,S$ with $Q$ a polynomial with unit leading coefficient and constant term $1$, relatively prime to the Fredholm series $S$ in $R\{\{T\}\}$. Then there is a continuous projector $p$, lying in the closure of $R[u]$, with $Q^{*}(u)\,w = p$ for some $w$ in that closure and $Q^{*}(u)^{\deg Q}(1-p) = 0$.
nodes.label: thm:riesz-coleman

nodes.statement: Put $\varphi' = 1 - Q^{*}(u)/Q^{*}(0)$, a compactoid operator. Theorem~\ref{thm:spectral-mapping} computes $\det(1 - T\varphi') = D(b_Q, \det(1-Tu))$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:dseries-goodzero} says that this has a good zero of order $\deg Q$ at $1$. Serre's projector at that zero (the construction behind Theorem~\ref{thm:riesz}) is $p$. Because the projector is produced as an operator-norm limit of polynomials in $\varphi'$, and $\varphi'$ is itself a polynomial in $u$, both $p$ and the inverse witness $w$ lie in the closure of $R[u]$ --- so they commute with $u$, not merely with $\varphi'$.

nodes.name: The full decomposition
nodes.statement: With the notation of Theorem~\ref{thm:riesz-coleman}, write $N = \ker Q^{*}(u)$. Then $M = N \oplus \mathrm{im}\,p$ topologically; $N$ is finitely generated projective of rank $\deg Q$ at every prime; $u$ is invertible on $N$; $\det(1-Tu \mid N) = Q$ and $\det(1-Tu\mid \mathrm{im}\,p) = S$; and $\mathrm{im}\,p$ is the unique $u$-stable closed complement on which $Q^{*}(u)$ is invertible.
nodes.label: thm:riesz-coleman-full

nodes.name: {\cite[Lemma 3.1]{Buzzard}}
nodes.statement: $Q$ and $S$ are relatively prime in $R\{\{T\}\}$ if and only if $Q^{*}(u)$ is invertible on the summand where the determinant is $S$.
nodes.label: lem:coprime-iff-unit

nodes.name: Determinants of summands
nodes.statement: If $u$ commutes with a continuous projector then its determinant is the product of the determinants of the two pieces; on a finitely generated summand the determinant is a polynomial, computed as the reversed characteristic polynomial of any matrix realisation.
nodes.label: prop:det-summand

nodes.statement: Write $\mathrm{charpolyRev}\,M = \det(1 - XM)$. It commutes with ring homomorphisms and satisfies Sylvester's identity $\det(1-XAB) = \det(1-XBA)$; an idempotent matrix with free range factors as $E = PQ$, $QP = 1$, and along such a factorisation $\mathrm{charpolyRev}\,M = \mathrm{charpolyRev}(QMP)$ whenever $ME = EM = M$. Over a field, if moreover $M = E - N$ with $N$ nilpotent then $\mathrm{charpolyRev}\,M = (1-X)^{\mathrm{rank}\,E}$.
nodes.label: lem:charpolyrev

nodes.statement: The index $N$ is \emph{dominant} for $F = \sum a_k T^k$ at radius $\rho$ if $\lVert a_k\rVert\rho^k \leq \lVert a_N\rVert\rho^N$ for all $k$, with strict inequality for $k > N$; that is, $N$ is Bella\"iche's largest integer minimising $v(a_n) - n\nu$ (\cite[Definition II.2.3]{Bellaiche}). A polynomial of degree $N$ dominant at $\rho$ with invertible leading coefficient is a \emph{$\rho$-dominant polynomial} (\cite[Definition II.2.4]{Bellaiche}).
nodes.label: def:dominant-index

nodes.statement: A $\rho$-dominant polynomial is exactly a Martin-distinguished element at radius $\rho$ (Definition~\ref{def:ismuldistinguished}); dominant polynomials are closed under multiplication.
nodes.label: lem:dominant-distinguished

nodes.name:
The slope factorisation, {\cite[Theorem II.3.6]{Bellaiche}};
                {\cite[Definition 2.2.5]{JN}}
nodes.statement: Let $F$ be entire over a Banach--Tate ring, with dominant index $N$ at radius $\rho$ and with $\lVert\cdot\rVert$ multiplicative on the dominant coefficient $a_N$. Then $F = PG$ with $P$ a $\rho$-dominant polynomial of degree $N$ and $G$ entire of dominant index $0$ at $\rho$; moreover $P$ and $G$ are relatively prime in $R\{\{T\}\}$.
nodes.label: thm:slope-factorisation

nodes.statement: Bella\"iche and Kedlaya \cite[Proposition 3.2.2]{Kedlaya} both run a Newton iteration $P_{l+1} = P_l + X_l$, $Q_{l+1} = Q_l + Y_l$ driven by the division estimates $\lVert f\rVert = \max(\lVert g\rVert\lVert q\rVert, \lVert r\rVert)$. We instead observe that those division estimates \emph{are} Martin's, so the hypotheses say exactly that $F$ is distinguished of order $N$ at radius $\rho$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:dominant-distinguished}); dividing $T^N$ by $F$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:wdivision}) and subtracting the remainder from $T^N$ produces the monic factor. This is Weierstrass preparation (Theorem~\ref{thm:wprep}) in the form needed. For coprimality (the norm-level form of \cite[Lemma 2.2.7]{JN}, and where \cite{JN} argue with resultants over the Gelfand spectrum): $\lVert G-1\rVert_\rho < 1$, so $G$ is a unit of the Tate algebra of radius $\rho$; dividing $G^{-1}$ by $P$ there gives $1 = Pq' + rG$ with $\deg r < N$, and the cofactor is entire because the entire division of $1 - rG$ by $P$ has the same quotient, by uniqueness. That is a B\'ezout identity for $P$ and $G$ in $R\{\{T\}\}$.

nodes.name: Two-sided weight bounds
nodes.statement: Suppose the matrix of $u$ satisfies $\lVert u_{ab}\rVert \leq \sigma^{\max(w(a) - w'(b),\,0)}$ for weights $w, w'$. Then $\lVert c_n(u)\rVert \leq \sigma^{f(n)}$ whenever $f(n) \leq \sum_{a\in S} w(a) - \sum_{a \in S} w'(a)$ for all $\lvert S\rvert = n$.
nodes.label: lem:two-sided

nodes.statement: A permutation $\pi$ of $S$ satisfies $\sum_{a\in S} w'(\pi a) = \sum_{a \in S} w'(a)$, so every Leibniz monomial of $\mathrm{minor}(u,S)$ carries the same column contribution and the row contribution is $\sum_{a\in S}w(a)$. This is the Hadamard bound of Lemma~\ref{lem:hadamard} with the column weight subtracted; note that nothing is inverted, so the estimate runs over an arbitrary complete ultrametric ring rather than a field.

nodes.name: Diagonal intertwining
nodes.statement: If $D\,M_v = M_u\,D$ entrywise for a diagonal $D$ with unit entries then $\mathrm{minor}(v,S) = \mathrm{minor}(u,S)$ for every finite $S$, and hence $\det(1-Tv) = \det(1-Tu)$. No compactness hypothesis and no inversion of $D$ is needed.
nodes.label: lem:diag-intertwine

nodes.name: Block-diagonal and rectangular block maps
nodes.statement: An operator $f$ on $c(I,R)$ induces the block-diagonal operator $\mathrm{blockDiag}\,f$ on $c(\sigma\times I, R)$, an equivalence if $f$ is; more generally a map $f : c(I,R) \to c(I',R)$ changing the fibre induces $\mathrm{blockMap}\,f$, and a family $T_{ij} : c(I,R)\to c(I',R)$ induces the rectangular block operator $\mathrm{blockOpMap}\,T$, with the expected composition rules against Proposition~\ref{prop:blockop}.
nodes.label: def:blockmaps

nodes.name: Perturbed unitriangular matrices are isometries
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be an infinite matrix over a complete ultrametric field with entries of norm $\leq 1$, unit diagonal, entries strictly below the diagonal of norm $\leq q < 1$, and finitely supported columns. Then $M$ defines an isometry of $c(\N,K)$ with dense range, hence a continuous linear equivalence.
nodes.label: thm:unitriangular

nodes.statement: Norm-preservation is a largest-index argument: in $Mx$ the coordinate at the largest index where $x$ attains its norm receives the unit diagonal contribution and nothing else of that size, the sub-diagonal entries being smaller by the factor $q$. Surjectivity is $q$-adic successive approximation.

nodes.name: Pairing of characteristic roots
nodes.statement: If $AB = c\cdot 1$ then $A$ is invertible with $B = c\,A^{-1}$, $\det A\det B = c^{\,n}$, and over an algebraically closed field $(\mathrm{charpoly}\,B).\mathrm{roots} = (\mathrm{charpoly}\,A).\mathrm{roots}$ mapped by $x \mapsto c/x$.
nodes.label: lem:charpoly-pairing

nodes.statement: $\Lhalo$ is realised coefficientwise, as \cite[proof of Corollary 3.18]{LWX} describes its elements: a two-sided stream $d : \Z \to \Zp$ with $v(d_j) \geq \max(0, -j)$, that is $\lVert d_j\rVert \leq p^{\min(0,j)}$, with pointwise addition, convolution product, and the gauge norm \[ \lVert d\rVert = \sup_{j\in\Z} \lVert d_j \rVert\, p^{-j} \in [0,1] . \]
nodes.label: def:haloint

nodes.statement: The constant embedding $\Zp \to \Lhalo$ is isometric; the element $T = \delta_1$ acts as the coefficient shift and satisfies $\lVert Tx\rVert = p^{-1}\lVert x\rVert$ exactly. Consequently \[ x \in T^{k}\,\Lhalo \iff \lVert x\rVert \leq p^{-k}, \] which is \cite[Lemma 3.15]{LWX} in the only form the estimate consumes.
nodes.label: prop:haloint-norm

nodes.name: Specialisation at a halo point
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a complete ultrametric field, $\psi : \Zp \to K$ an isometric ring homomorphism and $T_0 \in K$ with $p^{-1} < \lVert T_0\rVert < 1$. Then $\sum_{j\in\Z}\psi(d_j)T_0^{\,j}$ converges, and $d \mapsto d(T_0)$ is a continuous ring homomorphism $\Lhalo \to K$ satisfying $\lVert d(T_0)\rVert \leq \lVert T_0\rVert^{k}$ whenever $\lVert d\rVert\leq p^{-k}$.
nodes.label: def:halo-specialize

nodes.name: {The Banach--Tate ring $A = \Lhalo[1/T]$}
nodes.statement: Inverting $T$ gives the ring $A$ of streams satisfying a \emph{shifted} halo bound. It is complete for the gauge norm, contains $\Lhalo$ isometrically as its unit ball, and $T$ is a unit with $\lVert Tx\rVert = p^{-1}\lVert x\rVert$: a multiplicative pseudo-uniformizer. So $A$ is a Banach--Tate ring in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:istate}, and every element is $T^{-k}$ times an integral one.
nodes.label: prop:halotate

nodes.statement: Write $\Zp^{\times} = \Delta \times (1+p\Zp)$, $x = \omega_{\mathrm{T}}(x)\langle x\rangle$, with the Teichm\"uller lift $\omega_{\mathrm{T}}(x) = \lim_n x^{p^n}$; let $\ell\langle x\rangle = \tfrac1p\log\langle x\rangle \in \Zp$. For a nebentypus $\omega : (\Z/p)^{\times}\to\Zp^{\times}$ the \emph{universal character} of \cite[Notation 2.1]{LWX} is \[ [x] \;=\; \omega(\bar x)\,(1+T)^{\ell\langle x\rangle} \;\in\; (\Lhalo)^{\times}, \qquad (1+T)^{s} = \sum_{r\geq 0}\binom{s}{r}T^{r} . \] It is multiplicative and takes values in the unit ball.
nodes.label: def:univchar

nodes.statement: A function $f : \Zp\to\Zp$ has \emph{tilted degree $\leq n$} if $\lVert \tilde\Delta^{m}f(z)\rVert \leq p^{\,n-m}$ for all $m$ and all $z$, where $\tilde\Delta$ is the forward difference $f(z+1)-f(z)$.
nodes.label: def:tilteddeg

nodes.name: The calculus
nodes.statement: Tilted degree is monotone in $n$, additive under products, closed under convergent sums and pointwise limits, and constants have tilted degree $0$. The engine is the Leibniz rule $\tilde\Delta^{m}(fg) = \sum_{i+j=m}\tilde\Delta^{i}f \cdot (\tilde\Delta^{j}g)(\cdot + i)$, which is \cite[(3.5.1)]{LWX}, together with $\tilde\Delta\binom{z}{n} = \binom{z}{n-1}$, which is \cite[(3.5.2)]{LWX}.
nodes.label: lem:tilted-calculus

nodes.name: {\cite[Lemmas 3.12 and 3.13]{LWX}}
nodes.statement: If $f : \Zp\to p\Zp$ then $z\mapsto\binom{f(z)}{n}$ has tilted degree $\leq \lfloor n/p\rfloor$; and if $g(z) = \sum_k p^{k-1}(a_k/k)z^{k}$ has the shape of a normalised logarithm then $z\mapsto\binom{g(z)}{r}$ has tilted degree $\leq 0$.
nodes.label: lem:tilted-binomial

nodes.statement: A \emph{local matrix} is $\delta = \begin{pmatrix} a & b\\ c& d\end{pmatrix}\in M_2(\Zp)$ with $p \mid c$ and $d \in \Zp^{\times}$: the monoid $M_1$ of \cite[(2.3.3)]{LWX}. It has \emph{$U_p$-shape} if in addition $a \in p\Zp$, which is clause (3) of \cite[Proposition 3.1]{LWX}.
nodes.label: def:localmat

nodes.name: The entry stream, {\cite[Propositions 3.4 and 3.14]{LWX}}
nodes.statement: \cite[Proposition 3.4]{LWX} computes the matrix of a single $\Vert_\delta$ in the Mahler basis: \[ P_{m,n}(\delta) \;=\; \tilde\Delta^{m}\Bigl(\;\binom{\tfrac{az+b}{cz+d}}{n}\,[\,cz+d\,]\; \Bigr)\Big|_{z=0} . \] Expanding $[cz+d] = [d_0](1+T)^{g(z)}$ with $g(z) = \tfrac1p\log\bigl((cz+d)/d_0\bigr)$ gives the $T$-coefficient stream $r \mapsto [d_0]\,\tilde\Delta^{m}\bigl(\binom{f(z)}{n}\binom{g(z)}{r}\bigr)\big|_{z=0}$, and we take that stream as the definition of the entry $P_{m,n}(\delta)\in\Lhalo$.
nodes.label: def:entry

nodes.name: {\cite[Proposition 3.14(1)]{LWX}}
nodes.statement: For a local matrix of $U_p$-shape, \[ \bigl\lVert P_{m,n}(\delta)\bigr\rVert \;\leq\; p^{-(m - \lfloor n/p\rfloor)}, \qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad P_{m,n}(\delta) \in \mathfrak{m}^{\max(m-\lfloor n/p\rfloor,\,0)} . \] Without the shape hypothesis, that is for a general element of $M_1$, one still has $\lVert P_{m,n}(\delta)\rVert \leq p^{-(m-n)}$.
nodes.label: prop:entry-bound

nodes.statement: The $U_p$-shape makes $f(z) = (az+b)/(cz+d)$ take values in $p\Zp$, so $\binom{f(z)}{n}$ has tilted degree $\leq\lfloor n/p\rfloor$ by the first half of Lemma~\ref{lem:tilted-binomial}; $g$ is a normalised logarithm, so $\binom{g(z)}{r}$ has tilted degree $\leq 0$ by the second half; the product has tilted degree $\leq \lfloor n/p\rfloor$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:tilted-calculus}, and evaluating the definition of tilted degree at the $m$-th difference and $z=0$ is the claim. The constant $[d_0]$ is a unit.

A \emph{$U_p$-datum} on a class set $\iota$ consists of, for each $i\in\iota$, exactly $p$ summands, each given by a target index $\mathrm{tgt}(i,j)\in\iota$ and a local matrix $\mathrm{mat}(i,j)$ of $U_p$-shape. This is the content of \cite[Proposition 3.1]{LWX} that the estimate consumes; the column count of clause (2) is not needed. Assembling the entry streams block by block gives a matrix on $\iota\times\N$ and, by cofinite column decay, a continuous operator $D.\mathrm{op}$ on $c(\iota\times\N, \Lhalo)$.
nodes.label: def:updatum

nodes.statement: With $t = \lvert\iota\rvert$, set $\lambda(n) = \sum_{k<n}\bigl(\lfloor k/t\rfloor - \lfloor k/pt\rfloor\bigr)$.
nodes.label: def:lwxlambda

nodes.name: {\cite[Theorem 3.16]{LWX}}
nodes.statement: For every $U_p$-datum $D$ on a class set of size $t$ and every nebentypus $\omega$, the Fredholm determinant $\Char(P) = \sum_n c_n X^n$ of $D.\mathrm{op}$ is defined over $\Lhalo$ and \[ \lVert c_n\rVert \;\leq\; p^{-\lambda(n)}, \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad c_n \in T^{\lambda(n)}\,\Lhalo . \]
nodes.label: thm:lwx316

nodes.statement: Proposition~\ref{prop:entry-bound} says the matrix entry at $\bigl((i,m),(j,n)\bigr)$ has norm at most $p^{-\max(m-\lfloor n/p\rfloor,\,0)}$: a two-sided weight, with row weight $w(i,m) = m$ and column weight $w'(j,n) = \lfloor n/p\rfloor$. Lemma~\ref{lem:two-sided} therefore bounds $\lVert c_n\rVert$ by $p^{-f(n)}$ for any $f$ with $f(n)\leq \sum_{a\in S}w(a) - \sum_{a\in S}w'(a)$ over $n$-element $S$, and the combinatorial content is that $\lambda$ is such an $f$: on $\iota\times\N$ with $\lvert\iota\rvert = t$, the smallest possible value of $\sum_{(i,m)\in S}\bigl(m - \lfloor m/p\rfloor\bigr)$ over $\lvert S\rvert = n$ is attained by the first $n$ indices in the block order, which gives $\sum_{k<n}\bigl(\lfloor k/t\rfloor - \lfloor \lfloor k/t\rfloor/p\rfloor\bigr) = \lambda(n)$. Summability of the minors is the same estimate. Finally $T$-divisibility is Proposition~\ref{prop:haloint-norm}.

At a halo point $T_0$ with $p^{-1}<\lVert T_0\rVert<1$ set $\Char(P)(T_0) = \sum_n c_n(T_0)X^n \in K\llbracket X\rrbracket$. Its constant coefficient is $1$. The comparison slope sequence is $s_k = \bigl(\lfloor k/t\rfloor - \lfloor k/pt\rfloor\bigr)\cdot v(T_0)$, which is monotone.
nodes.label: def:speccharseries

nodes.name: {\cite[Corollary 3.18]{LWX}}
nodes.statement: For every $T_0$ in the boundary annulus, $v\bigl(c_n(T_0)\bigr) \geq \lambda(n)\,v(T_0)$, and the Newton polygon of $\Char(P)(T_0)$ lies on or above the polygon anchored at the origin whose $k$-th unit slope is $\bigl(\lfloor k/t\rfloor - \lfloor k/pt\rfloor\bigr)v(T_0)$.
nodes.label: thm:lwx318

nodes.statement: The coefficient bound is Theorem~\ref{thm:lwx316} pushed through the specialisation estimate of Definition~\ref{def:halo-specialize}. For the polygon statement, the constant coefficient is $1$ so the polygon is anchored at the origin, all coefficients have norm at most $1$ so the valuation sequence is admissible, and $\sum_{i<k}s_i = \lambda(k)\,v(T_0) \leq v(c_k(T_0))$ is the coefficient bound after taking logarithms; now apply the maximality clause of Definition~\ref{def:isnewtonpolygonof} to the comparison polygon of Definition~\ref{def:ofslopes}.

nodes.name: The equality clause of {\cite[Corollary 3.18]{LWX}}
nodes.statement: $v\bigl(c_n(T_0)\bigr) = \lambda(n)v(T_0)$ if and only if $b_{n,\lambda(n)} \in \Zp^{\times}$. Otherwise there is a definite margin: \[ v\bigl(c_n(T_0)\bigr) \;\geq\; \lambda(n)\,v(T_0) + \min\bigl(v(T_0),\, 1-v(T_0)\bigr). \]
nodes.label: thm:lwx-sharp

nodes.statement: The term-by-term estimate \cite[(3.18.1)]{LWX} shows that in $c_n(T_0) = \sum_m \psi(b_{n,m})T_0^{\,m}$ the term $m = \lambda(n)$ strictly dominates all others when $b_{n,\lambda(n)}$ is a unit: terms with $m < \lambda(n)$ are smaller because integrality forces $v(b_{n,m}) \geq \lambda(n)-m$, and terms with $m > \lambda(n)$ are smaller because $\lVert T_0\rVert<1$. An ultrametric sum with a unique dominant term has that term's norm. If $b_{n,\lambda(n)}$ is not a unit then every term loses either a factor $\lVert T_0\rVert$ or a factor $p^{-1}\lVert T_0\rVert^{-1}$, which is the stated margin.

Conjugate the matrix $P$ by $\mathrm{diag}(T^{\lfloor n/t\rfloor - \lfloor n/pt\rfloor})$, as \cite[proof of Theorem 3.16]{LWX} does, and transpose. The result is a compactoid operator on $c(\iota\times\N, A)$.
nodes.section: 10.7 Riesz theory at a halo vertex
nodes.label: def:tateop

nodes.statement: Principal minors are invariant under transposition and diagonal conjugation, so the Fredholm determinant of the operator of Definition~\ref{def:tateop} is $\Char(P)$ read in $A\llbracket X\rrbracket$.
nodes.section: 10.7 Riesz theory at a halo vertex
nodes.label: prop:tateop-det

nodes.statement: An index $n$ is a \emph{halo vertex} if $c_n = T^{\lambda(n)}\cdot(\text{unit})$ in $\Lhalo$. This is the situation of \cite[Remark 3.25]{LWX}; by Theorem~\ref{thm:lwx-sharp} it is implied by $b_{n,\lambda(n)}$ being a unit, that is, by the Newton polygon touching the lower bound at $n$.
nodes.section: 10.7 Riesz theory at a halo vertex
nodes.label: def:halovertex

nodes.name: Riesz decomposition at a halo vertex
nodes.statement: At a halo vertex $n$, the index $n$ is dominant for $\Char(P)$ at radius $p^{\lambda(n)-\lambda(n-1)}$ and the dominant coefficient is a multiplicative unit. Hence $\Char(P) = P_n\,G$ with $\deg P_n = n$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:slope-factorisation}), and Theorem~\ref{thm:riesz-coleman} gives the corresponding decomposition of $c(\iota\times\N, A)$: a $U_p$-stable summand of rank $n$ carrying exactly the first $n$ slopes, over the whole boundary annulus at once.
nodes.section: 10.7 Riesz theory at a halo vertex
nodes.label: thm:halo-riesz

nodes.statement:
Dominance at the stated radius is convexity of $\lambda$: the increments $\lfloor k/tfloor - \lfloor k/ptfloor$ are non-decreasing, so $\lambda(k) - k
u$ is minimised at $k = n$ for $
u$ the $n$-th increment, and the inequality is strict beyond $n$ because the increments grow. The coefficient bound of Theorem~ef{thm:lwx316} gives the inequality for $k 
eq n$ and the vertex hypothesis gives equality at $n$ together with multiplicativity of the norm on $c_n$, since $\lVert TVert$ is multiplicative and units of $\Lhalo$ are detected by their leading coefficient. Now apply Theorem~ef{thm:slope-factorisation} and then Theorem~ef{thm:riesz-coleman}.
nodes.section: 10.7 Riesz theory at a halo vertex

nodes.statement: Over a complete ultrametric field $K$ with $\lVert p\rVert<1$ and $p$ odd, $\log u = \sum_{n\ge0}(-1)^{n}\tfrac{(u-1)^{n+1}}{n+1}$ for $\lVert u-1\rVert<1$ and $\exp w = \sum_n w^{n}/n!$ for $\lVert w\rVert^{2}<\lVert p\rVert$. On the joint disc they are mutually inverse, and $\log$ is additive.
nodes.label: def:padicexplog

nodes.name: The $p$-adic binomial theorem at an arbitrary exponent
nodes.statement: For $e, x \in K$ with $\lVert x\rVert\leq c$, $\lVert e\rVert\lVert x\rVert\leq c$ and $c^{2}<\lVert p\rVert$, \[ \sum_{r\geq 0}\binom{e}{r}x^{r} \;=\; \exp\bigl(e\log(1+x)\bigr). \]
nodes.label: thm:padic-binomial

nodes.statement: Fix $x$ and regard both sides as power series in the exponent $e$, with geometrically decaying coefficients. They agree at every $e = n \in \N$, by the finite binomial theorem on the left and $\exp(n\log u) = u^{n}$ on the right. A power series vanishing at all natural numbers vanishes identically, by Strassman's theorem applied along $p^{k}\to 0$.

nodes.name: The binomial power identity
nodes.statement: $(1+T)^{p^{h}u} = \bigl((1+T)^{p^{h}}\bigr)^{u}$ for $u\in\Zp$; and $(1+T)^{p^{h}} - 1 \to 0$ as $h\to\infty$. Hence every halo point reaches the joint $\exp/\log$ disc at some analyticity level.
nodes.label: lem:pow-sub-one

nodes.statement: Both sides of the identity are continuous in $u$ and agree on $\N$, where they are the ordinary binomial theorem, and $\N$ is dense in $\Zp$. For the decay, iterate the one-step Kummer bound $\lVert (1+T)^{p}-1\rVert \leq \max(\lVert p\rVert\lVert T\rVert, \lVert T\rVert^{p})$, whose contraction factor is $\max(\lVert p\rVert, \lVert T\rVert^{p-1})<1$.

The specialisation of the universal character at $T_0$ is $\kappa_{T_0}(x) = \omega(\bar x)\,(1+T_0)^{\ell\langle x\rangle} = \omega(\bar x)\exp\bigl(s\log\langle x\rangle\bigr)$, with halo exponent $s = \log(1+T_0)/p$. On the sub-annulus $p^{-1}<\lVert T_0\rVert$, $\lVert T_0\rVert^{2}<p^{-1}$ it is an analytic weight in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:analyticweight}: the group is $\psi(\Zp^{\times})(1+p\calO_K)$, the level is the image of $M_1$, and the expansion of $\kappa_{T_0}(cz+d)$ on the closed unit ball is \[ (cz+d)^{2}\,\kappa_{T_0}(d)\sum_{m\geq 0}\binom{s}{m}\Bigl(\frac{c}{d}\Bigr)^{m}z^{m}, \qquad \text{decay } \rho = \lVert T_0\rVert\sqrt{p} . \]
nodes.label: def:haloweight

nodes.name: The halo weight at analyticity level $h$
nodes.statement: With $h = m-1$, $T'_h = (1+T_0)^{p^{h}}-1$ and $s_h = \log(1+T'_h)/p^{h+1}$, the character on the disc of radius $p^{-(h+1)}$ about a $\Zp$-unit $a$ is $x\mapsto [a](T_0)\exp\bigl(s_h\log(x/a)\bigr)$, an analytic weight at the level $M_1^{(h)}$ of matrices with $p^{h+1}\mid c$, of radius $\max(p^{-(h+1)}, \lVert T'_h\rVert)\sqrt p$.
nodes.label: def:haloweighth

nodes.statement: $C(\Zp,\Lhalo)$ with the action (2.3.2) of $M_1$, and $S^{D}_{\mathrm{int}}$ the corresponding space of automorphic functions at a tame level $U$ --- the same construction as Definition~\ref{def:forms}, at the ring $\Lhalo$ instead of a field.
nodes.label: def:intforms

nodes.name: {\cite[Proposition 3.4]{LWX}}
nodes.statement: The Mahler basis $\binom{z}{n}$ realises $C(\Zp,\Lhalo)$ as $c(\N,\Lhalo)$, and in these coordinates the matrix of $\Vert_\delta$ is exactly the entry stream $P_{m,n}(\delta)$ of Definition~\ref{def:entry}. The $T$-rescaled submodule $\widehat{\bigoplus}_n T^{n}\Lhalo\binom{z}{n}$ of \cite[(5.4.1)]{LWX} is realised by an explicit embedding.
nodes.label: prop:prop34

nodes.statement: Mahler's theorem applies because $\Lhalo$ is an ultrametric $\Zp$-Banach algebra. The Mahler coefficients of a function are its iterated forward differences at $0$, so the coefficient of $\binom{z}{n}$ in $\binom{z}{n'}\Vert_\delta$ is the $m$-th difference at $0$ of $\binom{f(z)}{n'}[cz+d]$, which is Definition~\ref{def:entry} verbatim; the $T$-expansion of $[cz+d]$ is the one performed there.

nodes.name: {\cite[(2.11.1)]{LWX} and \cite[Proposition 3.1]{LWX}}
nodes.statement: At a family of class representatives with trivial stabilisers, evaluation at the representatives is a bijection $S^{D}_{\mathrm{int}} \to c(\iota\times\N,\Lhalo)$; and for the genuine integral Hecke operator $[U\eta U]$ the diagram \[ \mathrm{ev}\circ[U\eta U] \;=\; D.\mathrm{op}\circ\mathrm{ev} \] commutes, where $D$ is the $U_p$-datum assembled from right-coset certificates of $U\eta U$. Its local matrices have $U_p$-shape because they lie in $\Iw_q\begin{pmatrix} p&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\Iw_q \subseteq \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix} p\Zp&\Zp\\ q\Zp&\Zp^{\times}\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$.
nodes.label: thm:prop31

nodes.statement: \cite[Proposition 3.1]{LWX} writes $\gamma_i v_j^{-1} = \delta_{i,j}^{-1}\gamma_{\lambda_{i,j}} u_{i,j}$ and finds $(U_p\varphi)(\gamma_i) = \sum_j \varphi(\gamma_{\lambda_{i,j}}) \Vert_{u_{i,j,p}v_j}$. That display is already proved in the ring-generic Hecke layer (Theorem~\ref{thm:evalatreps} and its companion for $[U\eta U]$), so what is left is to check that any operator satisfying it intertwines evaluation with $D.\mathrm{op}$, which is a computation with the block decomposition, and to verify the shape of $\delta_{i,j,p} = u_{i,j,p}v_j$ from the Iwahori double coset.

nodes.name: Level $m=1$
nodes.statement: At $m=1$ (so $p$ odd, $q=p$) the disc is the closed unit disc and the space is the Tate algebra $K\langle z\rangle = c(\N,K)$; the Colmez basis is $n!\binom{z}{n} = z(z-1)\cdots(z-n+1)$, a monic integral polynomial. Change of coordinates from the Colmez basis to the monomial basis is an isometry with dense range, hence a continuous linear equivalence, and \[ \mathrm{monomialToMahler} \;=\; \mathrm{diag}(m!)\circ\mathrm{colmezEquiv}^{-1} . \]
nodes.section: 11.3 Amice's theorem and the Colmez basis
nodes.label: prop:colmez-m1

nodes.name: {\cite[Lemme 1.4.9]{Colmez}}
nodes.statement: Let $g_n = \lfloor n/p^{h}\rfloor!\binom{z}{n}$ and let $a < p^{h}$ be a disc centre. The polynomial $g_{n,a}(w) = g_n(a+p^{h}w)$ has $\Zp$-coefficients, and factors as $g_{n,a} = c_{n,a}f_{n,a}$ where $f_{n,a}$ reduces mod $p$ to a monic polynomial of degree $\lvert K_{n,a}\rvert$, $K_{n,a} = \{k<n : k\equiv a \pmod{p^{h}}\}$, and $v(c_{n,a}) = \sum_{\ell=1}^{h}[\,a \bmod p^{\ell} < n\bmod p^{\ell}\,] \geq 0$.
nodes.section: 11.3 Amice's theorem and the Colmez basis
nodes.label: lem:colmez-valuation

nodes.statement: Each linear factor $a-k+p^{h}w$ is $p^{h}(w-(k-a)/p^{h})$ when $p^{h}\mid k-a$, and otherwise $(a-k)\bigl(1+p^{h}w/(a-k)\bigr)$; collecting the two kinds of factor gives the factorisation, and the valuation of the scalar is the count of carries, which is the displayed sum.
nodes.section: 11.3 Amice's theorem and the Colmez basis

nodes.name: Amice's theorem at level $h$
nodes.statement: Model $\mathcal{O}B_{p^{-h}}$, the functions analytic on every disc $a+p^{h}\Zp$ with the maximum of the $p^{h}$ Gauss norms, by $c(\Z/p^{h}\times\N, K)$ --- the Taylor coefficients on each disc in the coordinate $z = a+p^{h}w$. Then the map sending $e_n$ to the disc model of $g_n$ is an isometric equivalence $c(\N,K) \to c(\Z/p^{h}\times\N,K)$, and composing with $\mathrm{diag}(\lfloor n/p^{h}\rfloor!)$ turns Colmez coordinates into Mahler coefficients.
nodes.section: 11.3 Amice's theorem and the Colmez basis
nodes.label: thm:amice

nodes.statement: Order the basis by $n = (m(n)+1)p^{h} - i(n)$ with $1\leq i(n)\leq p^{h}$, and the discs by their centres, as \cite{Colmez} does; in that order Lemma~\ref{lem:colmez-valuation} says the reduction of the basis-change matrix is block upper triangular with each diagonal block lower triangular with invertible diagonal entries. Reindexing the columns by the involution reversing each block of $p^{h}$ consecutive integers turns the matrix into a perturbed unitriangular one, so Theorem~\ref{thm:unitriangular} applies. The two reindexings cancel, so the resulting map sends $e_n$ to $g_n$ on the nose. The final clause is the level-$h$ form of the statement that Mahler coefficients are forward differences of values at $\N$-points.
nodes.section: 11.3 Amice's theorem and the Colmez basis

nodes.name: The disc model of $S^{D,\dagger,m}$
nodes.statement: The action (2.3.2) does not preserve a single disc: it \emph{permutes} the discs. Writing $t_a(w) = a+p^{h}w$ and $a' = \delta(a)\bmod p^{h}$, the matrix identity $\delta\, t_a = t_{a'}\,\delta'$ with $\delta' = t_{a'}^{-1}\delta t_a$ of level $h$ says that the action carries the Taylor expansion on $a'$ to the one on $a$ through the single-disc weight action of Definition~\ref{def:haloweighth}. So the disc action is a block operator of $\kappa$-slashes permuted by $a\mapsto a'$, and it is a right action because the two data satisfy the cocycle rules. Everything in Chapter~\ref{chap:qmf} then transcribes: the space $S^{D,\dagger,m}$, evaluation at representatives, the Hecke operator, its compactness, its Fredholm determinant, and the eigenvalue reading of the zeros.
nodes.section: 11.3 Amice's theorem and the Colmez basis
nodes.label: def:discforms

nodes.name: {\cite[Proposition 2.17]{LWX}} at $m=1$
nodes.statement: On the sub-annulus $p^{-1}<\lVert T_0\rVert$, $\lVert T_0\rVert^{2}<p^{-1}$, the integral characteristic series evaluated at $T_0$ is the Fredholm determinant of $U_p$ on the overconvergent forms of the halo weight: \[ \Char(P)(T_0) \;=\; \det\bigl(1 - X\,[U\eta U]\bigr) \quad\text{on } S^{D,\dagger,1}_{\kappa_{T_0}}(U). \]
nodes.label: thm:lwx-prop217

nodes.statement: Four steps. (i) The specialised operator $P(T_0)$ on $c(\iota\times\N,K)$ has $c_n\bigl(P(T_0)\bigr) = c_n(P)(T_0)$, because specialisation is a continuous ring homomorphism (Definition~\ref{def:halo-specialize}) and the coefficients are limits of determinants of minors. (ii) The \emph{seam identity}: monomial-to-Mahler coordinates intertwine the analytic action of a certificate matrix with $P(T_0)$ --- both are $f\mapsto \chi(cz+d)f(\text{M\"ob}\,z)$ read at $\N$-points --- and hence blockwise for $[U\eta U]$.
